children.prompt: How can you tell which is larger? What is a useful strategy for comparing decimal numbers?

answer.short: Line up the decimal points and compare digits from left to right. At the first difference, the larger digit identifies the larger number.
answer.worked: Line up the decimal points. Compare the whole-number parts, then tenths, hundredths and subsequent places until the digits differ; add trailing zeros if helpful. The number with the larger digit at the first difference is larger. On a number line, it lies farther to the right.

classification.difficultyReason: Divide to identify recurring blocks, including cycles of six digits.

content.prompt: Express each fraction as a decimal.

answer.worked:
Divide $3$ by $7$. The successive digit calculations are:

$$\begin{align*}30&=7\times4+2\\20&=7\times2+6\\60&=7\times8+4\\40&=7\times5+5\\50&=7\times7+1\\10&=7\times1+3\end{align*}$$

The remainder returns to $3$, so the cycle repeats.

$$\frac37=0.428571428571\ldots=0.\dot42857\dot1$$

Divide $2$ by $11$:

$$\begin{align*}20&=11\times1+9\\90&=11\times8+2\end{align*}$$

The remainder returns to $2$, so $18$ repeats.

$$\frac2{11}=0.181818\ldots=0.\dot1\dot8$$

Divide $5$ by $12$:

$$\begin{align*}50&=12\times4+2\\20&=12\times1+8\\80&=12\times6+8\end{align*}$$

The remainder $8$ repeats, so the digit $6$ repeats.

$$\frac5{12}=0.41666\ldots=0.41\dot6$$

Divide $6$ by $13$:

$$\begin{align*}60&=13\times4+8\\80&=13\times6+2\\20&=13\times1+7\\70&=13\times5+5\\50&=13\times3+11\\110&=13\times8+6\end{align*}$$

The remainder returns to $6$, so $461538$ repeats.

$$\frac6{13}=0.461538461538\ldots=0.\dot46153\dot8$$

Divide $5$ by $6$:

$$\begin{align*}50&=6\times8+2\\20&=6\times3+2\end{align*}$$

The remainder $2$ repeats, so the digit $3$ repeats.

$$\frac56=0.83333\ldots=0.8\dot3$$

Divide $7$ by $12$:

$$\begin{align*}70&=12\times5+10\\100&=12\times8+4\\40&=12\times3+4\end{align*}$$

The remainder $4$ repeats, so the digit $3$ repeats.

$$\frac7{12}=0.58333\ldots=0.58\dot3$$

content.prompt: Recall that terminating decimals are produced from fractions with a denominator that is a product of powers of 2 and 5. List all the fractions with numerator 1 and denominator less than 100 that produce terminating decimals.

$\frac11,\frac12,\frac14,\frac15,\frac18,\frac1{10},\frac1{16},\frac1{20},\frac1{25},\frac1{32},\frac1{40},\frac1{50},\frac1{64},\frac1{80}$.

The denominator must have the form $2^a5^b<100$, where $a$ and $b$ are non-negative integers. Grouping by the power of 5 gives:

Higher powers of 5 are at least 125. Therefore the complete list is
$$\frac11,\frac12,\frac14,\frac15,\frac18,\frac1{10},\frac1{16},$$
$$\frac1{20},\frac1{25},\frac1{32},\frac1{40},\frac1{50},\frac1{64},\frac1{80}.$$

content.prompt: Explain why the cycle length of a recurring decimal corresponding to a fraction is always less than the denominator of the fraction.

answer.short: For denominator $n$, there are only $n-1$ possible nonzero remainders. A repeated remainder starts the same digit sequence again, so the cycle length is at most $n-1$, which is less than $n$.
answer.worked: Let the denominator be $n$. In long division, the possible nonzero remainders are $1,2,\ldots,n-1$. A zero remainder would make the decimal terminate. Each remainder determines the next digit and the next remainder, so when a remainder repeats, the digit sequence repeats too. There are only $n-1$ nonzero remainders, so the recurring cycle has at most $n-1$ digits. Therefore its length is less than $n$.

entries.description:
Comparing numbers by comparing the digits left to right
When using this method, it is important to write the numbers one underneath the other, with the decimal points lined up.
For example, to compare 3.78 and 3.612, we first write the numbers one beneath the other, aligning the decimal points.
3.78
3.612
Next, we compare the whole-number parts. Both are the same, so we proceed to the next digit or place.
We compare the tenths: 7 tenths is larger than 6 tenths. So 3.78 is larger than 3.612.
This method is the quickest and most straightforward method to use.

entries.description:
Writing a decimal correct to a number of decimal places
The rules for rounding are as follows. Suppose that we want to round 10.12589 correct to two decimal places.
• Identify the rounding digit in the second decimal place – in this case it is 2.
• Look at the next digit to the right of the rounding digit – in this case it is 5.
– If this next digit is 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4, leave the rounding digit alone.
– If this next digit is 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9, increase the rounding digit by 1.
In this case, the next digit is 5, so the rounding digit increases from 2 to 3.
• Now discard all the digits after the rounding digit.
Thus, we write 10.12589 as 10.13, correct to two decimal places.
